items.topic: Group A strep pharyngitis/scarlet fever — return to school after antibiotics when afebrile
items.client_needs_subcategory: Safety and Infection Prevention and Control
items.stem: A school-age child is diagnosed with group A streptococcal pharyngitis and starts appropriate antibiotics. When teaching the family about return to school or daycare, which instruction is most accurate?

options.text: Return only after completing the full 10-day antibiotic course, even if fever-free earlier
Return when afebrile and at least 12–24 hours after starting appropriate antibiotics (Ontario public health commonly uses 24 hours)
Return immediately after the first dose because strep is never contagious once diagnosed
Stay home for 2 weeks regardless of antibiotics to prevent rheumatic fever

rationales.A: Incorrect. Full course must be completed, but school return is typically allowed earlier once noninfectious criteria are met.
rationales.B: Correct. CDC: stay home until afebrile and at least 12–24 hours after starting appropriate antibiotics. Ontario public-health guidance commonly excludes until 24 hours after starting antibiotics.
rationales.C: Incorrect. Contagiousness declines after antibiotic therapy begins; immediate return after one dose is not the standard teaching.
rationales.D: Incorrect. Prolonged blanket exclusion is not required when antibiotics are started and the child is improving/afebrile.

sources.publisher: Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC)
sources.evidence: Stay home from work, school, or daycare until afebrile and at least 12–24 hours after starting appropriate antibiotic therapy.

items.stem: For a child starting antibiotics for confirmed group A strep pharyngitis, indicate whether each teaching point is Indicated or Not indicated.

rows.text: Keep the child home until afebrile and at least 12–24 hours after starting appropriate antibiotics (often taught as 24 hours in Ontario)
Complete the full prescribed antibiotic course even after symptoms improve
Practice hand hygiene and avoid sharing cups/utensils while contagious
Return to school immediately after the rapid strep test is positive, before antibiotics start
Stop antibiotics after 24 hours because the child is then cured

rationales.R1: Indicated. CDC and Ontario PHU align on delayed return until antibiotics have had time to reduce contagion and the child is afebrile/well enough.
rationales.R2: Indicated. Completing therapy reduces complications and treatment failure.
rationales.R3: Indicated. Hygiene and not sharing utensils reduce spread.
rationales.R4: Not indicated. Contagiousness persists until antibiotics have been started for the recommended interval.
rationales.R5: Not indicated. Feeling better after 24 hours does not mean the full course can be stopped.

items.jurisdiction_note: Health Canada fit guidance + CDC helmet effectiveness
items.topic: Bicycle helmet — properly fitted helmet every ride
items.stem: A parent asks how to best protect a child from serious head injury while bicycling. Which teaching is most accurate?

options.text: Wear a properly fitted bicycle helmet, fastened, every time the child rides
Helmets are unnecessary if the child rides only on sidewalks
Buy a helmet several sizes too large so the child can "grow into" it
A cracked helmet is fine to reuse if the outer shell still looks mostly intact

rationales.A: Correct. CDC: properly fitted bicycle helmets every ride reduce head/brain injury risk. Health Canada: well-fitted, activity-matched helmets protect against serious head injury.
rationales.B: Incorrect. Serious crashes can occur off roadways; helmets are recommended whenever riding.
rationales.C: Incorrect. Health Canada: helmets should not be large enough to grow into; fit must be snug now.
rationales.D: Incorrect. Bike helmets are single-impact devices and should be replaced after impact or if damaged.

items.topic: Infant IM injection — vastus lateralis (anterolateral thigh)
items.stem: The nurse prepares an intramuscular injection for a 6-month-old infant. Which site is preferred?

options.text: Vastus lateralis muscle of the anterolateral thigh
Dorsogluteal muscle of the buttock as first choice
Deltoid muscle for all infants under 12 months as first choice
Any subcutaneous fat pad because IM sites are unused in infancy

rationales.A: Correct. OpenStax CNS: for children <18 months, vastus lateralis is preferred as the most developed muscle. CDC: for most infants, vastus lateralis (anterolateral thigh) is the recommended IM vaccine site.
rationales.B: Incorrect. Buttock injections are avoided in infants/children due to sciatic nerve injury risk.
rationales.C: Incorrect. Deltoid is not the preferred first-choice IM site for young infants with limited deltoid mass.
rationales.D: Incorrect. Many infant vaccines/medications require true IM administration into muscle.

items.topic: Enteral tube feeding — elevate HOB 30–45° to reduce aspiration
items.stem: A client is receiving intermittent nasogastric tube feedings. Which nursing action best reduces the risk of aspiration pneumonia?

options.text: Keep the head of the bed elevated about 30° to 45° during feeding and for a period afterward as tolerated
Place the client flat supine for the entire feeding to promote gastric emptying
Omit tube-placement checks because aspiration cannot occur with a correctly ordered formula
Encourage the client to lie on the left side with the head down during bolus feeds

rationales.A: Correct. OpenStax Med-Surg: maintain HOB 30°–45° to reduce aspiration risk. Merck: sit upright 30°–45° during tube feeding and 1–2 hours afterward to minimize aspiration pneumonia.
rationales.B: Incorrect. Flat positioning increases aspiration risk.
rationales.C: Incorrect. Placement and intolerance assessments remain essential; aspiration is a major complication.
rationales.D: Incorrect. Head-down positioning worsens aspiration risk.

sources.title: 19.3 Parenteral and Enteral Nutrition
sources.evidence: Most serious complication is respiratory aspiration; maintain head of bed at 30° to 45° unless contraindicated; assess placement/intolerance.

sources.title: Enteral Nutrition
sources.evidence: Patients should sit upright at 30 to 45° during tube feeding and for 1 to 2 hours afterward to minimize aspiration pneumonia.

items.topic: Spiritual care — facilitate chaplain/clergy per client preference
items.stem: A hospitalized client asks to speak with a spiritual advisor from their faith tradition. What is the nurse's best action?

options.text: Facilitate contact with the hospital chaplain or the client's preferred clergy and protect quiet time for spiritual practices as able
Tell the client that spiritual needs are outside nursing responsibility and refuse to help
Impose the nurse's own prayer tradition without asking about the client's preferences
Advise the client to wait until discharge because spiritual care is never part of inpatient care

rationales.A: Correct. OpenStax Fund: support patients within their faith tradition; many agencies have chaplains; offer clergy/quiet prayer time based on patient preferences. Merck: interdisciplinary palliative teams include chaplains to relieve spiritual distress.
rationales.B: Incorrect. Spiritual support is a legitimate nursing/caring responsibility.
rationales.C: Incorrect. Care must center the client's beliefs, not the nurse's.
rationales.D: Incorrect. Spiritual care is appropriate during hospitalization.

items.topic: Hospice care — comfort and dignity focus, not curative treatment
items.stem: A family asks how hospice care differs from aggressive curative treatment for a terminally ill relative. Which statement by the nurse is most accurate?

options.text: Hospice focuses on comfort, dignity, and quality of life rather than treatments aimed at curing the disease
Hospice requires stopping all medications, including those used for pain or dyspnea
Hospice is identical to intensive curative chemotherapy protocols
Hospice can be used only in intensive care units and never at home

rationales.A: Correct. OpenStax: hospice is comfort care at end of life and does not involve treatments aimed at curing the disease. Merck: hospice focuses on comfort and meaningfulness, not cure or extending life.
rationales.B: Incorrect. Symptom-relief medications are central to hospice comfort care.
rationales.C: Incorrect. Hospice is not curative intensive treatment.
rationales.D: Incorrect. Hospice is commonly provided at home as well as other settings.

items.topic: Mixing insulin — draw clear short-acting before cloudy NPH
items.stem: A nurse must mix regular (clear) insulin and NPH (cloudy) insulin in one syringe as ordered. Which technique is correct?

options.text: Draw the clear short-acting insulin into the syringe first, then the cloudy NPH
Draw the cloudy NPH first, then push any extra mixture back into the clear vial
Shake both vials vigorously until foamy before drawing either dose
Mix insulin glargine with NPH in the same syringe for convenience

rationales.A: Correct. MedlinePlus: when mixing two insulins, draw the short-acting (clear) dose first, then the longer-acting (cloudy) dose. OpenStax: NPH is cloudy; most other insulins are clear.
rationales.B: Incorrect. Drawing cloudy first risks contaminating the clear vial; mixed insulin should not be pushed back into vials.
rationales.C: Incorrect. NPH should be gently rolled, not shaken hard into foam/clumps.
rationales.D: Incorrect. Long-acting analogs such as glargine are not mixed with other insulins.

sources.title: Giving an insulin injection
sources.section: Filling the Syringe — two Types of Insulin
sources.evidence: NPH is cloudy and rolled (not shaken). Draw short-acting first, then longer-acting; do not push mixed insulin back into a vial.

sources.title: 28.2 Insulin and Non-Insulin Injectable Diabetes Drugs
sources.section: Types of Insulin — NPH cloudy; long-acting agents
sources.evidence: Insulins are typically clear except NPH (cloudy). Long-acting agents (e.g., glargine) provide basal coverage; mixing rules exclude combining incompatible long-acting products with others.
